newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms want stronger defense for takeovers.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms want stronger defense for takeovers.

text.p: Indian industrialists on Thursday cheered a new takeover code introduced by the country's stock market regulator, but said they needed new rules to prepare themselves against hostile bids.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) last month approved a new takeover code for companies.
"The code should be adopted and be in place latest by the end of the month," SEBI chairman, D.R. Mehta told a seminar on the takeover code.
Industrialists said Indian firms should be allowed to buy back their shares and be given access to low-interest bank funds to finance takeovers.
But Mehta said bank financing for companies to consolidate their holdings was unlikely to be permitted in the near future.
"Until I get the same facilities as my counterpart abroad, some protection must be built in," leading industrialist S.K. Birla said.

He was referring to the fact that multinational companies and non-resident Indians had access to funds at a lower interest cost. They are also permitted to offer shares of companies as collateral against loans unlike Indian firms.

"Obviously, it is easier for a foreign company to takeover an Indian company than the other way around," said a paper by seminar organisers the Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
The paper recommended that domestic companies be allowed to borrow from abroad at comparitively lower rates of interest to consolidate their shareholding.
"If you are allowing Indian businessmen to takeover companies, you should allow them access to international money," said K.K. Modi, vice-president of FICCI.
Leading industrialist R.P Goenka said the buy back of shares was essential for domestic firms to defend themselves.
"If you allow buy back, the existing management would feel comfortable," Goenka said.
"I'm not scared of competition. I'm scared if you bind my hands behind my back," he said.
M.S. Verma, managing director of the country's largest commercial bank the State Bank of India said firms should not try to change the rules before they even started playing the game.
"If we have started the whole process of liberalisation and foreign participation, let us set out rules and play by those rules. Let us not cry foul before the game has begun," he said.
Verma agreed that banks should lend Indian companies money to finance takeovers.
"It has not been allowed so far but there is no reason why it should not be given serious thought," he said.
Nick Butt, head of corporate finance at Jardine Fleming India Broking, said unsolicited takeover offers would become more frequent over time.
He said Indian companies were vulnerable in the current code which gave them only 21 days to react to takeover offers.
A weak Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practises Act and lack of transparency about shareholder patterns also made it difficult for them to defend themselves against hostile bids, Butt said.
"Indian companies should not wait for the bid but take action ahead of unsolicited offers and be prepared," he advised.
